title: Rethinking agrivoltaic incentive programs: A science-based approach to encourage practical design solutions
abstract: Agrivoltaic systems are promising solutions to address global food and energy challenges by combining agriculture and solar photovoltaics. However, the lack of appropriate regulations to define and guide their implementation constrains the growth of agrivoltaic systems in the U.S. This study uses a shading and radiation tool to evaluate an existing agrivoltaic incentive program that defines agrivoltaic designs based on shading reduction limits and panel height requirements. Our analysis indicates that structuring policy requirements around shading, and not light availability, may lead to an underestimation of crop suitability by neglecting diffuse radiation. Furthermore, we show that agrivoltaic systems can avoid increasing panel height if policy acknowledges use-case scenarios where farming only occurs between rows. In light of these insights, this study proposes two key policy recommendations: (1) benchmark crop suitability based on daily light integral (DLI) requirements for a shade-intolerant crop selected to represent a prevalent crop in the region, and (2) include an incentive scenario where agriculture is only required between rows. These two recommendations can potentially incentivize designs that are practical and closer in cost to conventional solar farms, thereby accelerating the adoption of cost-effective agrivoltaic systems.

## Rethinking agrivoltaic incentive programs: A science-based approach to encourage practical design solutions

## Henry J. Williams , Yipu Wang , Bo Yuan , Haomiao Wang , K. Max Zhang[*]

_Sibley School of Mechanical and Aerospace Engineering, Cornell University, Ithaca, NY 14853, United States_

## **1. Introduction**

The solar photovoltaics (PV) industry is rapidly expanding to satisfy global energy needs and ambitious climate goals. However, as the number of large-scale solar farms increases, so do concerns about their environmental [1] and community impacts [2], including land use conflict with agriculture [3], aesthetic alterations of the rural landscape [4], and potential changes to a region’s primary industry [5]. Agrivoltaics, the concept of co-locating solar energy and agriculture, is a promising solution to these challenges, with several environmental benefits, including improved water use efficiency in arid regions [6], microclimate regulation for crops [7], and potential improvements in

productivity due to beneficial shading [8]. Furthermore, agrivoltaics can potentially protect crops from climate change [9], with benefits reported for several designs in regions including Belgium [10], France [11], and Arizona [12]. However, while agrivoltaics systems demonstrate numerous benefits, economic and logistic barriers limit widespread implementation, particularly for agrivoltaic designs that greatly deviate from conventional solar farm height, spacing, and panel placement. Along with these challenges, agrivoltaic design tools and government incentives are still in the early phases of formation in the U.S., providing limited guidance for solar developers.

Several examples of agrivoltaic policies exist worldwide, with requirements typically focused on preserving agricultural production. In Japan, agrivoltaic systems must produce at least 80% agricultural yield

In Germany, the requirement is 66% of reference yield [14], and in France, installations must produce at least 90% yield compared to a nearby control plot [15]. Italy requires that PV panels cover no more than 40% of area in agrivoltaic sites [16]. Some policies also include requirements for PV installations. In Japan, panels must be mounted at least 2 m (6.6 ft) in height [17]. Germany outlines two scenarios for agrivoltaics—one where panels are mounted at least 2.1 m (6.9 ft) in height (Category I), and another where panels are mounted under 2.1 m (6.9 ft) in height (Category II) [14]. For Category I, crops can be planted everywhere except where the racking systems enter the ground. For Category II, an option remains to plant crops only between rows of panels. This provides flexibility for solar developers and farmers by considering several design scenarios that can fit a variety of agricultural needs. In the U.S., flexibility is paramount, as the risk associated with the nascency of agrivoltaics presents a major barrier to solar developers adopting dual-use systems [18].

The Massachusetts Department of Energy Resources (DOER) is leading the development of agrivoltaic incentives in the U.S. with the Solar Massachusetts Renewable Target (SMART) program, which subsidizes agrivoltaic development with compensation rates up to $0.06/ kWh [19]. To participate in the SMART program, an agrivoltaic site must meet strict design requirements, including 10 ft. (3.0 m) minimum panel height (measured at horizontal position) for horizontal single-axis tracking (HSAT) and 8 ft. (2.4 m) minimum panel height for fixed tilt systems, maximum 5 MWAC rated capacity, and no more than 50% shade in any given location within the solar site compared to baseline field conditions as determined by a “shading-only” tool developed for DOER SMART program assessment [20].

Although the SMART program shading restrictions and height limits are intended to ensure adequate agricultural integration, they may limit site designs to costly options due to two primary gaps. First, the SMART program may underestimate agricultural suitability because the “shading-only” tool does not account for diffuse radiation that contributes to PAR intensity in shaded areas. Sharing solar radiation between solar arrays and co-located crops is a critical component of agrivoltaic designs. Direct radiation, which comes from the sun in a direct line, is intercepted by solar panels. Diffuse radiation, on the other hand, is scattered by atmospheric constituents and present in shade. Crops respond to both direct and diffuse radiation in the photosynthetically active radiation (PAR) range. Thus, considering both direct and diffuse radiation to predict ground-level PAR is critical to estimating crop suitability [21]. Second, the underlying assumption for the SMART program is that agricultural activities will occur everywhere on site, but in reality, farmers might be unwilling to accept the risk involved in

operating large farming equipment directly underneath panels. If no planting occurs underneath panels, shading and panel height requirements might be unnecessary for those regions. In this case, panel height requirements would be detrimental to project profitability, as more steel would be needed for elevated racking systems. With structural costs already surpassing $18/W [22], corresponding to over 18% of total project investment, it is critical to minimize additional structural costs for agrivoltaic systems to be economically competitive with traditional solar PV.

To provide a comprehensive evaluation of agrivoltaic site requirements under the SMART program, it is necessary to first consider direct and diffuse radiation with a field-validated modeling tool, then use agronomic knowledge of ground-level radiation conditions to estimate crop suitability. A brief review of related work is presented as follows.

Several computational models have been developed to compare ground-level direct and diffuse radiation conditions created by various PV module types [23], racking configurations [24], and site locations [25] for agrivoltaics. PVLIB, for example, is an open-source toolbox developed by Sandia National Laboratory [26] that models direct and diffuse radiation conditions [27,28]. Other models have been repurposed from other fields, such as MIR, MUSC, RADBAL (MMR) [29], a light balance calculation tool used to compare tracking and fixed solar PV implications for ground-level radiation conditions [30]. Another example is Autodesk Ecotect Analysis, an architecture-oriented tool used to estimate PAR levels [31]. The software, which is now discontinued, was previously used to estimate conditions for various solar farm designs, including tracking systems, different mounting heights, and tilt angles [32]. Furthermore, Radiance [33] is a general-purpose raytracing software that accounts for reflected radiation [34] and can be coupled with geometric modeling to predict bifacial agrivoltaic system performance [35]. For bifacial modeling, either ray tracing or view factor can be used to estimate reflected radiation on the backside of the solar modules. Both Fraunhofer Institute for Solar Energy Systems ISE and the National Renewable Energy Laboratory (NREL) have developed Radiance-based raytracing bifacial software [36,37]. Finally, several agrivoltaic studies have utilized Zemax [38], a commercial optical software, to evaluate the performance of novel panel designs in agrivoltaics [39–41]. However, for agrivoltaic applications, existing simulation strategies need to be modified to estimate ground-level crop suitability based on shading and radiation conditions in a 3D environment.

Given simulated ground-level direct and diffuse radiation, crop photosynthesis and biomass accumulation can be estimated assuming negligible canopy height and no other limiting factors such as water

availability or soil nutrient content [42]. Crop suitability analysis is key to estimating the agricultural capacity of dual-use systems, as limited light availability is an underlying design challenge in agrivoltaics. One strategy to evaluate crop photosynthesis is to use photosynthetic photon flux density (PPFD), which quantifies the number of photons in the photosynthetically active radiation (PAR) spectrum incident on a surface per unit time [43]. PPFD has been widely used for making real-time decisions in controlled environment agriculture [44]. In agrivoltaic studies, a crop-specific PPFD saturation level, known as the light saturation point (LSP), has been used to predict crop suitability [45]. However, a crop canopy typically saturates at a higher level than an individual leaf [46], meaning that LSP-based estimates might underpredict overall crop suitability. Instead, the daily integral of PPFD has been shown to predict plant growth and biomass yield more accurately than peak light flux for a fully developed canopy [47]. To account for duration and intensity, the daily light integral (DLI) can be calculated as a function of PPFD and photoperiod, thus measuring the total PAR intensity received in a day [48]. Crop suitability can then be estimated using crop-specific DLI requirements, which are readily available from controlled environment agriculture data [49].

Inspired by challenges and opportunities in the Massachusetts SMART Program, we present the Agrivoltaic Radiation Tool (ART), a 3D shading and radiation model that tailors established solar PV modeling methods to agrivoltaic system design and regulatory measures. ART demonstrates how ground-level shading and radiation should be jointly considered for defining agrivoltaic systems, and how policy can encourage cost-effective, purpose-built agrivoltaic designs by considering agricultural operation logistics. Findings suggest that SMART Program guidelines might result in over-engineered site designs that are less effective in practice than on paper. Namely, shading and height requirements may lead to costly designs that are not, in practice, fully utilized for agricultural production both underneath and between solar arrays. With these considerations, this study recommends improving future agrivoltaic incentive programs.

Our study addresses an imperative need to investigate policy requirements with appropriate design tools by using a shading and radiation model to identify key gaps in an existing incentive program.

Proposed modifications aim to broaden opportunities in incentive programs for cost-competitive agrivoltaic options by encouraging compromise between agricultural operations and solar farm design.

## **2. Methods**

## _2.1. Overview of the Agrivoltaic radiation tool (ART)_

ART is an agrivoltaic modeling tool that utilizes ray-tracing methods with direct and diffuse hourly radiation inputs to estimate crop suitability based on DLI requirements for specific crops. ART generates shading conditions for a 3D solar farm design by estimating the direct radiation blocked by solar modules, similar to the SMART shading tool [50]. ART then utilizes equations based on PVLIB and other raytracing tools but extends them to calculate ground-level PAR intensity or PPFD. Thus, ART improves upon the SMART shading tool by incorporating direct and diffuse radiation and extends PVLIB’s modeling capabilities by introducing 3D shade conditions. In doing so, ART estimates ground-level light availability for a given solar farm design, considering height and spacing effects. Furthermore, ART can generate crop-specific agricultural maps, indicating areas with and without sufficient DLI for full crop production. These features are needed for creative agrivoltaics designs, such as an existing system in Grafton, MA that removes every third pair of panels, creating a scenario that requires a 3D model to accurately characterize ground-level shading and radiation conditions. Other scenarios that require a 3D model include sites where plant-to-panel and panel-to-plant shading are significant factors, sites where edge effects are important, and sites that combine solar arrays oriented at perpendicular axes (Fig. 1). While this study utilizes the 3D capabilities to simulate the Grafton site, future studies will leverage ART to simulate other examples presented in Fig. 1.

Table 1 compares the main features of ART, the SMART shading tool, PVLIB, and Bifacial Radiance, which is a ray-tracing tool developed by NREL with 3D capabilities and ground-level irradiance calculations not specific to the PAR spectrum [33].

## _2.4. Crop suitability and input data_

To evaluate crop suitability for policy incentives, ART calculates DLI and ranks each pixel from unsuitable to optimum based on benchmark ranges for specific crops. DLI is the product of PPFD and photoperiod, where photoperiod is given as the total time from sunrise to sunset. In this study, crop suitability rankings are based on DLI requirements for the tomato, representing a shade-intolerant crop grown in Massachusetts, where 520 total acres were harvested in 2022 [52,53]. Specifically, DLI over 20 mol/(m[2] -day) is considered suitable for tomatoes, and above 30 mol/(m[2] -day) is optimum [54]. Similar to how the SMART program’s 50% rule might represent a lower-bound shade requirement, benchmarking crop suitability with a shade-intolerant crop’s DLI requirement should not limit light availability for other crops, thereby enabling crop selection flexibility throughout the lifespan of a facility. Unlike the SMART Program’s 50% rule, however, the DLI requirement more closely represents crop photosynthesis and biomass accumulation by using accumulated PAR intensity instead of shading alone. Crop suitability is also calculated for lettuce, a shade-tolerant crop, and strawberries, whose DLI requirements lie between tomatoes and lettuce. These results are presented in S2 in the Supplementary materials.

ART generates ground-level PPFD for each year between 1998 and 2020 to evaluate performance for agrivoltaic systems using historical data from the National Solar Radiation Database (NSRDB) [55]. The results are ranked based on ground-level PPFD, then the median year is selected for further modeling based on the P50 statistical analysis for evaluating future conditions with 50% confidence [56].

## _2.5. Design scenarios_

As mentioned, the Massachusetts SMART program provides the first statewide agrivoltaic incentives in the Northeastern U.S., using a shading-only simulation tool to support and guide agrivoltaic design decisions. The SMART Program requires every location on site to exhibit less than 50% shading compared to open field conditions, and the program sets strict height requirements, including 8 ft. (2.4 m) minimum height for fixed tilt systems and 10 ft. (3.0 m) minimum height for tracking [20]. Using ART, this section evaluates the effectiveness of those requirements and provides recommendations for future agrivoltaic incentive programs.

Three racking types are used to illustrate potential policy changes based on ART results: fixed tilt with two panels in portrait (2P Fixed; 2PF), HSAT with one panel in portrait (1P Tracking; 1PT), and HSAT with two panels stacked in portrait (2P Tracking; 2PT). This study

## **3. Results and discussion**

## _3.1. Model evaluation_

Solar farm field data is used to evaluate the capabilities of ART in calculating ground-level PPFD. The field data is collected using a PAR sensor placed equidistant between two adjacent rows of solar panels in a fixed-tilt south-facing site in Ithaca, New York. Thus, the sensor experiences a combination of sun and shade throughout the day, providing an opportunity to evaluate both total and diffuse radiation conditions. As ART aims to simulate the overall performance of agrivoltaic sites over extended periods, average values for simulated and measured are compared for model evaluation, referred to as the mean difference (MD). Normalized mean bias error (NMBE) is also used to evaluate the simulated results to measured results [59]:

where _Mi_ are measured values and _Si_ are simulated values. A positive NMBE indicates that the simulation tool overestimates results, while

Model evaluation is presented in Fig. 3, where Global Horizontal Irradiation (GHI) from historical reanalysis weather datasets is used as input. The model achieves an R[2 ] value of 0.83. The MD and NMBE between simulated and measured PPFD are 30.54 μmol/m[2] -s and 6.64%, respectively.

To ensure ART’s ability to simulate varied conditions, the model is also evaluated, in terms of both daily-averaged and hourly-averaged PPFD, over an extended 20-day period using sensors at various locations at the solar facility in Ithaca, NY [60]. Furthermore, the model is evaluated using Ithaca airport weather station data (approximately 4 mi away from the solar facility) as input. These evaluations, presented in Section S1 in the Supplementary materials, assure that ART performs adequately over a growing season. In all cases, historical weather data is utilized to evaluate the model’s simulation ability, and not necessarily the predictive ability. In further studies, evaluation of the model’s predictive capability using predicted weather data will give more insight into the model’s ability to capture predicted conditions.

## _3.2. Analyzing the SMART program site requirements_

To analyze the SMART program site requirements, design scenarios presented in Table 2 are simulated in ART and evaluated based on shading and crop suitability percentages. Results are shown in Table 3, where shading and crop suitability percentages are calculated in regions indicated by red dashed boxes in Figs. 4–6 to eliminate edge effects. Based on P50 results, 2017 is selected for analysis as it best predicts future conditions. Reported shading results include the maximum shading percentage for the entire site (i.e., SMART Program methodology) and the maximum shading percentage between rows. Reported

crop suitability results include suitable area percentage under and between rows of solar arrays, as well as the percentage of the area considered to be optimum for crop growth based on DLI requirements for tomatoes. The “A” scenarios meet the SMART shading and height requirements, and these designs are ideally suitable to integrate agricultural activities everywhere. Large equipment could move between rows, and the area beneath rows could be suitable for crops that are hand-harvested. The “B” scenarios do not meet SMART requirements, but these designs would be suitable for growing crops between rows based on crop suitability indices as defined by tomato DLI requirements. In addition to tomatoes, crop suitability results for lettuce and strawberries are presented in Section S2 in the Supplementary materials. These results demonstrate that designing a system around a baseline shade intolerant crop, such as tomatoes, ensures that crops with higher shade tolerance, such as lettuce and strawberries, will have their DLI requirements satisfied in the design.

## _3.2.1. 2P fixed tilt (2PF)_

Fig. 4 shows results for 2PF-A and 2PF-B. 2PF-A, which is modeled after a SMART Program site in Grafton, MA, meets SMART program shading and height requirements with the removal of every third panel pair. As a result, every location is suitable for crop growth, at the cost of extra steel on a per-panel-basis (one third fewer panels on the steel racking) and reduced power production (every third panel pair was removed) compared to no panels removed. 2PF-B meets shading requirements between rows, but panel height and shading underneath rows would eliminate 2PF-B from SMART requirements. However, if crops are only planted between rows, 2PF-B would be a suitable design, with 100% of the area between rows meeting the lower-bound tomato DLI threshold and 74.4% of that area falling in the “optimum” range with a 2 ft. buffer on either side of the panel edges.

## _3.3. Policy implications_

## _3.3.1. SMART policy recommendations_

Our analysis indicates two major challenges with the SMART Program requirements. Firstly, neglecting diffuse radiation means the SMART Program’s 50% shade requirement is a conservative cutoff. For example, in 2PT-B, 51.8% maximum shade between rows is suitable for shade-intolerant crop species based on DLI requirements. Secondly, the SMART Program limits site design flexibility by assuming that agricultural activities will occur everywhere on site when in practice crops might only be planted between rows to avoid large equipment operating beneath rows. Thus, in the case that crops are only planted between rows, panel height requirements and under-panel shading limits would not necessarily improve agricultural compatibility, and the panel height requirements would serve to increase project costs, as more steel would be needed for elevated racking systems.

Two key policy modifications could minimize these shortcomings in future incentives. Firstly, the shade requirement could be abandoned in favor of DLI-based suitability criteria for a shade-intolerant crop, such as tomatoes, which would maintain the simplicity of the shade cutoff while being more realistic for crop suitability by considering direct and diffuse radiation accumulated daily. Secondly, agrivoltaic definitions could be divided into two categories based on planting location. The first category could incorporate panel height requirements case-by-case to enable agriculture everywhere on site, and the second category could eliminate panel height requirements for sites that intend to only plant agriculture between rows. These two modifications could reduce the cost of entry for solar developers and accelerate the adoption of agrivoltaics in Massachusetts by tailoring incentive requirements to practical agricultural considerations rather than applying a blanket rule for all installations.

## _3.3.2. Potential policy implementation challenges_

Several barriers could present challenges to implementing the two recommended policy modifications. Firstly, while a DLI-based suitability criteria aims to broaden the range of agrivoltaics designs in the incentive program, it still requires the use of a simulation tool for acceptance into the incentive program. This could potentially be a constraint limiting future flexibility of agrivoltaics design options, particularly as agrivoltaics crop trial field data becomes more in the coming years, potentially allowing stakeholders to learn from a combination of verified field data and simulation tools. Thus, an incentive program should remain flexible and adaptive to new data as it becomes available.

Secondly, incorporating a design category for planting agriculture only between rows presents questions regarding land use, as this concept potentially reduces farmers’ income from agriculture, and would require more land for the same amount of electricity if panels are spaced at greater intervals to accommodate more agricultural production between. This constraint presents opportunities for future research in optimizing panel spacing to maintain sufficient crop production without significantly increasing land requirements for solar PV. In this study, the design scenarios favor maintaining row spacing similar to conventional (non-agrivoltaic) solar PV designs, such as 5.0 m (16.4 ft) spacing for 2PF, 4.0 m (13.1 ft) spacing for 1PT, and 6.0 m (19.7 ft) spacing for 2PT (Table 2).

## **4. Conclusions**

Agrivoltaic systems are growing in popularity, and government incentives will play an important role in guiding the designs of future systems. In this paper, we present the Agrivoltaic Radiation Tool (ART) and use it to demonstrate how a current incentive program can be

improved to meet the dynamic needs of agriculture given various site configurations. Based on findings from several design scenarios, we present the following recommendations for future agrivoltaic incentive programs to encourage the adoption of agrivoltaics by reducing the need for excess material for increasing panel heights and adding gaps between panels. Introducing this approach to agrivoltaic incentive programs will reward creative and cost-competitive agrivoltaic designs, accelerating solar PV development while reducing land-use conflict with agriculture. Estimating crop suitability based on light availability neglects the effects of temperature, water availability, and other physiological stresses. Thus, in cases where soil-water parameters are known, a comprehensive analysis of crop suitability potential can include more factors. For solar farm design, a financial model is needed to quantify the tradeoffs between panel height and agricultural activity in agrivoltaic sites. This study relies on a qualitative assumption that lower panel heights will reduce steel consumption, and therefore reduce material and construction costs. Furthermore, this study evaluates an agrivoltaic incentive program from a crop-growing agrivoltaics approach. More research is needed to investigate potential modifications needed to optimize incentives for animal grazing, and more agrivoltaic crop field trials are needed to evaluate suitability index predictions presented in this study. Lastly, from a crop suitability perspective, an ideal policy would consider several ranges of DLI corresponding to various crops, from shade-intolerant to shade-tolerant, as well as seasonal DLI profiles, considering lower DLI early and late in the growing season and higher DLI during the summer months. However, policymakers might have challenges enforcing requirements based on specific crops and seasonal DLI profiles, hence why this study proposes to define a shade-intolerant crop to represent a lower limit for crop suitability averaged over a growing season. Future policy might consider long-term farming plans, if possible, to design sites specifically for different agricultural activities.
